title: Perfume and silver (Mark 14:1–11)
hookLine: a woman anoints him with costly nard; Judas goes to the priests
carry: she has done a beautiful thing

cards: Two days before the Passover. In Jerusalem, the chief priests and scribes want a quiet way to arrest Jesus, but not during the feast, they say, or the people will riot.

Out in the village of Bethany, Jesus is at dinner in the house of a man called Simon the leper. A woman comes in carrying an alabaster jar of perfume, pure nard, very expensive. She doesn't dab a little.
She breaks the jar and pours the whole thing over his head. The smell fills the house. Every conversation stops.
Somebody is already doing the math.

teach.b: Some at the table are indignant. Why this waste? It could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor.
And they scold her. Jesus says, in the King James Bible: "Let her alone; why trouble ye her? she hath wrought a good work on me."
The Greek word for good there, kalos, also means beautiful. She has done a beautiful thing. Then: the poor you always have with you, and you can do them good whenever you want.
He's echoing Moses, who said the poor shall never cease out of the land, and so, open your hand to them. In Deuteronomy, that line is a reason to give, not an excuse.
Here it's about this moment: you will not always have me.

She has done what she could, he says; she has anointed my body beforehand for burying. Remember the word Christ, the anointed one? Here, in Mark, someone anoints him at last, and he says it's for his burial.
Wherever the good news is told in the whole world, he promises, what she has done will be told in memory of her. Yet Mark never tells us her name.
John's Gospel, telling a similar scene, names her Mary, the sister of Martha and Lazarus. Then Mark cuts sharply to someone he does name.
Judas, one of the twelve, goes to the chief priests to hand him over.

teach.h: SHE HATH WROUGHT A GOOD WORK ON ME.
teach.b: They're glad, and promise him money. Perfume poured out for love. Silver taken for a betrayal.

how: Christians often read this story at the start of Holy Week; many churches use anointing oil in baptism, confirmation or prayer for the sick, and Christians remember the unnamed woman as an example of extravagant devotion.

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: broke the jar and poured it

s: Mark tells us the woman's name
Mark leaves her unnamed. John's similar scene names her Mary.
the onlookers priced the perfume at over three hundred denarii
"more than three hundred pence," in the King James. they wanted it sold for the poor.
Mark says Judas was paid thirty pieces of silver
Mark says only that they promised him money. thirty pieces is Matthew's detail.

games.q: you're at the table when a woman pours a whole jar of costly perfume over Jesus's head. the others are scolding her. what does Jesus say?
o: she should have sold it for the poor.
let her alone; she has done a beautiful thing.
games.why: "Let her alone; why trouble ye her? she hath wrought a good work on me." and wherever the gospel is told, she will be remembered.

practice: Think of someone you love, and what it would look like to do something extravagant for them: not practical, just beautiful, like a whole afternoon, a letter that takes an hour, or showing up in person when a text would do.
Notice the voice that says what a waste, listen to it kindly, and picture doing it anyway. If you pray, offer that love to God too.

wordCard.voice: Kalos, the Greek word for good, which also means beautiful. A woman pours out costly nard for love, and Judas goes to take silver for a betrayal.

orig.note: Greek: good, fine, beautiful. behind the King James "good work" in Mark 14:6.

carryVoice: Your line: she has done a beautiful thing. And it's told in memory of her. See you tomorrow.
